sectionTitle: Yield and atom economy of chemical reactions (chemistry only)

specStatements.text: Even though no atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, it is not always possible to obtain the calculated amount of a product because:
the reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible
some of the product may be lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture
some of the reactants may react in ways different to the expected reaction.
The amount of a product obtained is known as the yield. When compared with the maximum theoretical amount as a percentage, it is called the percentage yield.
% Yield= (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) ×100
calculate the percentage yield of a product from the actual yield of a reaction
(HT only) calculate the theoretical mass of a product from a given mass of reactant and the balanced equation for the reaction.

The atom economy (atom utilisation) is a measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is important for sustainable development and for economic reasons to use reactions with high atom economy.
The percentage atom economy of a reaction is calculated using the balanced equation for the reaction as follows:
(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) ×100
calculate the atom economy of a reaction to form a desired product from the balanced equation

(HT only) explain why a particular reaction pathway is chosen to produce a specified product given appropriate data such as atom economy (if not calculated), yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products.

scopeNotes.statement: (HT only) calculate the theoretical mass of a product from a given mass of reactant and the balanced equation for the reaction.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The specification restricts the calculation of a theoretical mass to Higher tier. Every percentage yield item written for both tiers therefore states the maximum theoretical mass in the stem; the student is never required to derive it. Only the three items tiered 'higher' (q08, q09, q10) ask for a theoretical mass to be worked out from a reactant mass and the balanced equation.

scopeNotes.statement: from a given mass of reactant and the balanced equation for the reaction
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Higher tier theoretical mass items print the balanced equation and the relative atomic or relative formula masses needed, and give the mass of reactant, exactly as the specification specifies. No item asks students to write or balance the equation themselves here, to work backwards from a product mass to a reactant mass, or to identify a limiting reactant from two given masses.

scopeNotes.statement: given appropriate data such as atom economy (if not calculated), yield, rate, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Pathway comparison items are Higher tier only and print every figure the comparison needs. Students are never expected to recall industrial conditions, catalysts, plant costs or reaction mechanisms; the reasoning asked for is confined to weighing the printed data, which is what the specification names.

scopeNotes.statement: The percentage atom economy of a reaction is calculated using the balanced equation for the reaction
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Every atom economy item supplies the balanced equation and the relative formula masses. Atom economy is never calculated from measured experimental masses, and it is always stated for a named desired product, because the specification's equation takes the relative formula mass of the desired product from the equation.

scopeNotes.statement: calculate the percentage yield of a product from the actual yield of a reaction
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Percentage yield items ask for the percentage yield itself, given the actual yield, and use the equation in the form the specification prints it. No item requires the equation to be rearranged to find an actual mass or a theoretical mass from a percentage, which the specification does not ask for.

concepts.definition: The mass of product that would be obtained if every one of the reactant particles reacted in the way the balanced equation shows and none of the product was lost. It is the largest mass that could possibly form, so it is the figure the actual mass is compared with.
The amount of a product obtained from a reaction. It is the amount actually made and collected, measured after the product has been separated from the reaction mixture.
The yield compared with the maximum theoretical amount, expressed as a percentage. It measures how much of the possible product was actually obtained in that particular preparation.

% Yield = (Mass of product actually made) / (Maximum theoretical mass of product) x 100. The mass actually made goes on the top and the maximum theoretical mass on the bottom, so the answer can never exceed 100%.

concepts.term: Reversible reaction as a reason for a lower yield
concepts.definition: The reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible. Reactants are still present when the amounts stop changing, so less product forms than the equation predicts.

Some of the product may be lost when it is separated from the reaction mixture, for example crystals left on filter paper, solution left in a beaker, or solid left behind on transfer. The product still exists, but it is not weighed.
Some of the reactants may react in ways different to the expected reaction, forming products other than the one wanted. Those atoms are then unavailable for the desired product, so its yield falls.

concepts.term: Conservation of atoms and a yield below 100%
concepts.definition: No atoms are gained or lost in a chemical reaction, yet the calculated amount of product is not always obtained. The atoms still exist, but some are in unreacted reactants, in a different product, or in product that was never collected.

A measure of the amount of starting materials that end up as useful products. It is worked out from the balanced equation, so it is a property of the reaction chosen rather than of how well the experiment was carried out.

It is important for sustainable development and for economic reasons to use reactions with high atom economy: less of the starting material ends up as waste that must be treated or disposed of, and less raw material is bought for each tonne of useful product.

(Relative formula mass of desired product from equation) / (Sum of relative formula masses of all reactants from equation) x 100. Both figures are read from the balanced equation, including the balancing numbers.

The desired product is the substance the reaction is being carried out to make; any other product is a by-product. Atom economy is always quoted for a stated desired product, so the same reaction has different atom economies depending on which product is wanted.

A number written in front of a formula multiplies the whole of that relative formula mass. In Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2 the desired product term is 2 x 56 = 112 and the reactant total is 160 + (3 x 28) = 244.

concepts.term: Theoretical mass from a balanced equation
concepts.definition: Divide the given mass of reactant by its relative formula mass, use the balanced equation to convert to the amount of product, then multiply by the relative formula mass of the product. This gives the maximum theoretical mass of that product.

Where more than one reaction makes the same product, the pathway chosen is judged on data such as atom economy, yield, rate, the position of any equilibrium and the usefulness of the by-products, not on any single one of these figures alone.

concepts.term: Percentage yield compared with atom economy
concepts.definition: Percentage yield measures how much of the possible product a particular preparation actually delivered. Atom economy measures how much of the starting material the equation itself sends into the desired product. A reaction can be high in one and low in the other.

A by-product that can be sold or used elsewhere means less of the starting material is truly wasted, so a pathway with a modest atom economy may still be chosen. The by-product does not change the atom economy figure for the desired product.

misconceptions.question: No atoms are gained or lost in a reaction, so why is less product collected than the calculation predicts?
misconceptions.correct: All the atoms still exist. They are simply not all in the collected product: the reaction may not have gone to completion because it is reversible, some product was lost when it was separated from the mixture, or some reactants reacted in ways different to the expected reaction.
misconceptions.misconception: If I end up with less product than the equation predicts, some of the atoms must have been used up or destroyed along the way.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is learnt as a rule about a sealed flask, so when the balance reads short of the prediction students look for missing matter rather than for matter that is somewhere else.
misconceptions.correction: Ask where the atoms are, not whether they exist. Name the three places the specification allows: still unreacted in the mixture, left behind on the filter paper or glassware, or locked into a different product.

misconceptions.question: A reaction is written with a reversible arrow. Does that mean no product is obtained?
misconceptions.correct: Product is obtained, but the reaction may not go to completion because it is reversible, so reactants are still present at the end and the yield is below the maximum theoretical amount.
misconceptions.misconception: In a reversible reaction the products all turn straight back into reactants, so in the end you get nothing out of it.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The double arrow is read as 'it goes backwards', and going backwards is pictured as a complete undoing rather than as a forward and a backward change happening in the same mixture.
misconceptions.correction: Read the arrow as 'both directions at once'. The mixture at the end contains product and reactant together, which is why the yield is reduced rather than zero.

misconceptions.question: Crystals are left on the filter paper and stuck to the beaker. Has mass been destroyed?
misconceptions.correct: No. The crystals left behind still exist, they are just not on the balance. The actual yield falls and so does the percentage yield, but no atoms have been gained or lost.
misconceptions.misconception: Losing product when you filter or transfer it means mass has not been conserved, so the law of conservation of mass does not really hold in practicals.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet conservation of mass and percentage yield in the same practical and merge them: any reading lower than expected is taken as evidence against the law rather than as product left in the apparatus.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two ideas. Conservation of mass is about atoms in the reaction; percentage yield is about how much of the product reached the balance.

misconceptions.question: Burning methane in a limited supply of air also makes carbon monoxide. What has happened to the yield of carbon dioxide?
misconceptions.correct: It falls, because some of the reactants have reacted in a way different to the expected reaction. Those carbon atoms are in carbon monoxide instead, so they cannot appear in the carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: If a substance that is not in the equation turns up, those atoms have been lost from the reaction altogether.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The equation is treated as a complete description of what a mixture must do, so any other product is filed as an error or a loss rather than as a competing reaction with its own products.
misconceptions.correction: Treat every unexpected product as a second destination for the same atoms. Nothing is lost; the atoms are shared between two reactions, so the wanted one gets fewer.

misconceptions.question: A reaction should make 8.0 g of product and 6.4 g is obtained. Which way round does the division go?
misconceptions.correct: Mass actually made divided by maximum theoretical mass, times 100: 6.4 / 8.0 x 100 = 80%.
misconceptions.misconception: Divide the bigger number by the smaller one so the sum works out neatly, giving 8.0 / 6.4 x 100 = 125%.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Division is remembered as 'big number first' from earlier arithmetic, and the equation is recalled as a pair of masses rather than as a fixed ratio of actual to theoretical.
misconceptions.correction: Anchor the equation to its meaning: the answer is the fraction of the possible product that was made, so the possible mass must be underneath.

misconceptions.question: Can a percentage yield be greater than 100%?
misconceptions.correct: No. The maximum theoretical mass is the most that could possibly form, so the mass actually made cannot exceed it. A figure above 100% means the product was weighed before it was dry or pure, or the theoretical mass was calculated wrongly.
misconceptions.misconception: If you work really carefully you can get more product than the equation predicts, so a yield above 100% is just a very good result.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Percentage yield is treated as a score for practical skill, and scores can be beaten. The word 'maximum' in the equation is skimmed over.
misconceptions.correction: Point back at the word maximum. The theoretical mass assumes every atom goes where it is wanted and nothing is lost, so it is a ceiling that careful work approaches but cannot pass.

misconceptions.question: Are percentage yield and atom economy two names for the same measure?
misconceptions.correct: No. Percentage yield compares the mass of product actually made with the maximum theoretical mass. Atom economy compares the relative formula mass of the desired product with the sum of the relative formula masses of all the reactants in the balanced equation.
misconceptions.misconception: They are both percentages about how much product you get out of a reaction, so they must mean the same thing.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both are taught in the same section, both are percentages, and both are described loosely as being about 'how much product you get', which hides the fact that one is measured and one is calculated from the equation.
misconceptions.correction: Sort them by where the numbers come from: yield comes off a balance after an experiment, atom economy comes off the balanced equation before anyone does anything.

misconceptions.question: Would working more carefully and losing less product raise the atom economy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Atom economy is calculated from the balanced equation alone, so it is fixed for a given reaction. Working more carefully raises the percentage yield; only choosing a different reaction changes the atom economy.
misconceptions.misconception: Spilling less, filtering better and washing the crystals properly will push the atom economy up.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Atom economy is met straight after percentage yield, which really does depend on technique, so the same practical explanation is carried over to a quantity that never touches the laboratory.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what data the calculation needs. It needs only formulae and relative formula masses, so nothing that happens at the bench can appear in the answer.

misconceptions.question: For Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2, do the large numbers in front of the formulae go into the atom economy calculation?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. The desired product term is 2 x 56 = 112 and the reactant total is 160 + (3 x 28) = 244, giving 112 / 244 x 100 = 45.9%.
misconceptions.misconception: The big numbers in front of formulae are only there to balance the equation, so you use the relative formula masses on their own.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Balancing is practised as a puzzle about atom counts and then set aside, so the coefficients are seen as bookkeeping rather than as quantities that multiply the masses.
misconceptions.correction: Read 3CO aloud as 'three lots of CO'. If three lots go in, three lots of relative formula mass go into the sum.

misconceptions.question: Iron comes from the iron(III) oxide, so can the atom economy be worked out from that reactant alone?
misconceptions.correct: No. The bottom of the equation is the sum of the relative formula masses of all the reactants from the equation, so the carbon monoxide must be included: 160 + (3 x 28) = 244.
misconceptions.misconception: Only the reactant that contains the atoms of the desired product counts, so divide by the relative formula mass of that one substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students trace the wanted atoms back to their source and stop there, because the other reactant feels like a helper rather than a starting material that also had to be bought.
misconceptions.correction: Every reactant is a starting material the process consumes. Atom economy measures the fraction of everything put in that comes out as the desired product.

misconceptions.question: 25 g of calcium carbonate is heated: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Is the theoretical mass of calcium oxide also 25 g?
misconceptions.correct: No. 25 g of CaCO3 (Mr 100) is 0.25 mol, which gives 0.25 mol of CaO (Mr 56) = 14 g. The remaining 11 g leaves as carbon dioxide.
misconceptions.misconception: Mass is conserved, so the mass of product must come out the same as the mass of reactant you started with.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation of mass is remembered as 'mass in equals mass out' and then applied to one product rather than to all the products together.
misconceptions.correction: Conservation applies to the whole equation. Add every product, including any gas that escapes, and the total does match the reactants.

misconceptions.question: For 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO, does the 2 in front of MgO mean the answer should be doubled?
misconceptions.correct: No. The equation gives 2 mol of MgO from 2 mol of Mg, a 1 : 1 ratio. 4.8 g of Mg (Ar 24) is 0.2 mol, so 0.2 mol of MgO (Mr 40) forms, which is 8.0 g.
misconceptions.misconception: There is a 2 in front of the product, so whatever the calculation gives has to be multiplied by 2 at the end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The balancing numbers are applied one at a time instead of as a ratio, so the number in front of the product is used without checking the number in front of the reactant.
misconceptions.correction: Always write the ratio from both sides before converting: 2 mol Mg gives 2 mol MgO, which cancels to 1 : 1, so no doubling is involved.

misconceptions.question: Is the pathway with the highest atom economy always the one a manufacturer chooses?
misconceptions.correct: No. The choice weighs atom economy against the yield, the rate, the position of any equilibrium and how useful the by-products are. A high atom economy route that is slow or reaches equilibrium at a low yield may be rejected.
misconceptions.misconception: Atom economy is the modern, greener measure, so the route with the best atom economy is automatically the right one.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Atom economy is introduced alongside sustainable development, which gives it a moral weight that makes it feel like the deciding figure rather than one of several.
misconceptions.correction: Work through the data in the question one line at a time. A pathway is chosen on the whole set of figures the question supplies, and the specification names five of them.

misconceptions.question: A reaction has an atom economy of 100%. Must its percentage yield be 100% as well?
misconceptions.correct: No. N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3 with an atom economy of 100%, because every reactant atom is in the ammonia, yet the reaction is reversible and does not go to completion, so the percentage yield is much lower.
misconceptions.misconception: If the atom economy is 100% then every atom really does end up in the product, so nothing can be missing at the end.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A 100% atom economy is read as a statement about what happened rather than about what the equation allows, so the ceiling is mistaken for the outcome.
misconceptions.correction: Atom economy says where the atoms could go if the reaction did exactly what the equation says. Yield says how much of that actually happened.

misconceptions.question: A reaction makes the desired product and a by-product the company sells. Should the by-product go on the top of the atom economy calculation?
misconceptions.correct: No. The top line is the relative formula mass of the desired product from the equation only. A saleable by-product may be a good reason to choose the reaction, but it does not change the atom economy for that product.
misconceptions.misconception: The by-product is useful too, so add its relative formula mass to the top of the calculation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The definition is remembered as 'materials that end up as useful products', and a by-product that is sold obviously is useful, so it is swept into the numerator.
misconceptions.correction: Fix the desired product first, then apply the equation exactly. Report the usefulness of the by-product separately, as a reason for choosing the pathway.

misconceptions.question: Would leaving a reversible reaction running for much longer eventually give a 100% yield?
misconceptions.correct: No. A reversible reaction reaches a point where reactants and products are both present and the amounts stop changing, so waiting alone does not convert all the reactants.
misconceptions.misconception: A reversible reaction is really just a slow one, so give it enough time and every reactant will be converted.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Incomplete reaction is confused with slow reaction, because in most reactions students meet, waiting longer really does finish the job.
misconceptions.correction: Distinguish how fast from how far. A reversible reaction stops changing before all the reactants have been used, however long it is left.

misconceptions.question: CaCO3 (Mr 100) -> CaO (Mr 56) + CO2. Does 25 g of calcium carbonate give 56 g of calcium oxide?
misconceptions.correct: No. The relative formula masses give the ratio, not the masses themselves. 25 g is a quarter of 100, so a quarter of 56 g forms, which is 14 g.
misconceptions.misconception: The relative formula masses in the equation are the masses in grams, so the answer is just the relative formula mass of the product.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The line '100 gives 56' is written down during teaching and remembered as a pair of masses rather than as a scaling factor to be applied to the mass in the question.
misconceptions.correction: Always scale. Write the equation masses underneath the formulae, then multiply both by the same factor to reach the mass given in the question.

misconceptions.question: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Does this reaction have one atom economy?
misconceptions.correct: No. Atom economy is quoted for a stated desired product. For calcium oxide it is 56 / 100 x 100 = 56%; for carbon dioxide it is 44 / 100 x 100 = 44%.
misconceptions.misconception: Each reaction has a single atom economy, so it does not matter which product you put on the top line.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Atom economy is presented as a property of a reaction, like its rate, so the phrase 'desired product' in the equation is read as a label rather than as a choice that changes the answer.
misconceptions.correction: Name the desired product before starting the calculation, and quote the answer with that product named.

mcqs.stem: A student calculates that 8.0 g of copper sulfate crystals should form, but obtains 6.2 g after filtering, washing and drying. Which statement best explains the shortfall?

options.text: Some of the product was left behind when it was separated from the mixture.
options.rationale: One of the three reasons the specification gives: product lost during separation is never weighed, so the actual yield falls below the theoretical maximum.

options.text: Some atoms were destroyed as the reaction took place, so less product formed.
options.rationale: Chosen by students who read a shortfall on the balance as matter disappearing rather than as matter left elsewhere.

options.text: Mass is conserved only when the reaction is carried out in a sealed vessel.
options.rationale: Picked by students who think a practical loss disproves the law, so they add a condition the law does not have.

options.text: The relative formula mass used for the crystals must have been too large.
options.rationale: Students who assume the practical was faultless look for the error in the arithmetic instead of in the apparatus.

mcqs.stem: An industrial reaction is written with a reversible arrow. Why does this reduce the yield of the product?

options.text: The reaction runs backwards instead, so no product is obtained at all.
options.rationale: The double arrow is read as complete reversal, which turns a reduced yield into no yield.

options.text: The reaction does not go to completion, so reactants remain at the end.
options.rationale: The specification's first reason: a reversible reaction may not go to completion, so some reactant is never converted.

options.text: The yield is fine if the mixture is simply left to run for much longer.
options.rationale: Incomplete reaction is confused with slow reaction, so time is offered as the cure.

options.text: The product decomposes into substances that are not shown in the equation.
options.rationale: A plausible-sounding chemical reason, but it describes a different, unexpected reaction rather than reversibility.

mcqs.stem: A student transfers a precipitate from the filter paper to a watch glass and some is left on the paper. What happens to the percentage yield?

options.text: It rises, because the maximum theoretical mass used becomes smaller.
options.rationale: Comes from muddling which mass sits on which line of the equation.

options.text: It is unchanged, because no atoms can be lost in a chemical reaction.
options.rationale: Conservation of mass is applied to the balance reading, so a practical loss seems impossible.

options.text: It falls, because the mass of product actually made is now smaller.
options.rationale: The top of the equation is the mass actually obtained, so product left behind lowers it while the theoretical mass is unchanged.

options.text: It cannot be found until the precipitate left behind has been weighed.
options.rationale: Students who treat the calculation as needing a full mass audit stall rather than use the mass they have.

mcqs.stem: Methane burned in a limited supply of air produces some carbon monoxide as well as carbon dioxide. Why is the yield of carbon dioxide lower than expected?

options.text: Carbon atoms are lost from the system when carbon monoxide is formed.
options.rationale: An unexpected product is treated as a loss of atoms rather than as a second destination for them.

options.text: The reaction is reversible, so carbon dioxide changes back into methane.
options.rationale: Reversibility is offered for any reduced yield, whether or not the reaction is reversible.

options.text: Carbon monoxide has a smaller relative formula mass than carbon dioxide.
options.rationale: A true statement that explains nothing; students often pick the option they can verify.

options.text: Some of the reactants have reacted in a way different to the expected one.
options.rationale: The specification's third reason: atoms taken by a competing reaction cannot appear in the desired product.

mcqs.stem: What does the percentage yield of a reaction compare?

options.text: The mass of product actually made with the maximum theoretical mass.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition: the yield compared with the maximum theoretical amount, as a percentage.

options.text: The mass of the desired product with the total mass of all reactants.
options.rationale: This is the atom economy comparison, offered by students who merge the two measures.

options.text: The maximum theoretical mass with the mass of product actually made.
options.rationale: The correct pair of masses in the wrong order, which gives figures above 100%.

options.text: The mass of the useful product with the mass of the waste products.
options.rationale: A reasonable-sounding 'useful versus wasted' framing that matches neither definition.

mcqs.stem: The maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide is 8.0 g. A student obtains 6.4 g. What is the percentage yield?

options.rationale: 8.0 / 6.4 x 100, from dividing the larger mass by the smaller one.
6.4 / 8.0 x 100 = 80%, actual mass over maximum theoretical mass.
Chosen by students who reason that atoms cannot be lost, so the yield must be complete.
The percentage not obtained, from 1.6 / 8.0 x 100; the shortfall is calculated instead of the yield.

mcqs.stem: A preparation has a maximum theoretical mass of 3.6 g. After filtering, 2.7 g of dry product is collected. What is the percentage yield?

options.rationale: 3.6 / 2.7 x 100, from putting the theoretical mass on top.
Selected by students who believe filtering cannot really lose product because mass is conserved.
The proportion lost rather than the proportion obtained.

mcqs.stem: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Relative formula masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of calcium oxide from 25 g of calcium carbonate?

options.rationale: From assuming conservation of mass means the product has the same mass as the reactant.
The relative formula mass of the product quoted as a mass in grams, with no scaling.
25 x 100 / 56, from inverting the ratio of relative formula masses.
25 / 100 = 0.25 mol CaCO3, giving 0.25 mol CaO, and 0.25 x 56 = 14 g.

mcqs.stem: 2Mg + O2 -> 2MgO. Ar(Mg) = 24, Mr(MgO) = 40. What is the maximum theoretical mass of magnesium oxide from 4.8 g of magnesium?

options.rationale: 4.8 / 24 = 0.2 mol Mg, and the 2 : 2 ratio gives 0.2 mol MgO, so 0.2 x 40 = 8.0 g.
From doubling the answer because of the 2 in front of MgO, ignoring the 2 in front of Mg.
From assuming the product must weigh the same as the magnesium used.
The relative formula mass of magnesium oxide quoted directly as the mass formed.

mcqs.stem: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr(Fe2O3) = 160, Ar(Fe) = 56. What is the maximum theoretical mass of iron from 320 g of iron(III) oxide?

options.rationale: From ignoring the 2 in front of Fe and treating the ratio as 1 : 1.
320 / 160 = 2 mol Fe2O3, which gives 4 mol Fe, and 4 x 56 = 224 g.
From applying the 3 in front of CO2 to the iron as well.
From assuming the mass of product equals the mass of reactant used.

mcqs.stem: What does the atom economy of a reaction measure?

options.text: The amount of the theoretical product that is obtained in practice.
options.rationale: This is percentage yield; the two measures are routinely merged.

options.text: How carefully the product was separated from the reaction mixture.
options.rationale: Atom economy is treated as a verdict on laboratory technique.

options.text: The amount of the starting materials that ends up as useful products.
options.rationale: This is the specification's definition of atom economy, also called atom utilisation.

options.text: The share of the atoms in the product taken from the main reactant.
options.rationale: A plausible reading of the words 'atom economy' that inspects the product rather than the inputs.

mcqs.stem: Why is it important to use reactions with a high atom economy?

options.text: The percentage yield of the reaction is then certain to be high as well.
options.rationale: The two percentages are assumed to move together, so one is read off the other.

options.text: It shows that the product has been separated without any loss occurring.
options.rationale: Atom economy is mistaken for a measure of how well the practical was done.

options.text: It means the reaction will reach completion much more quickly than others.
options.rationale: Rate is imported into a calculation that says nothing about how fast a reaction goes.

options.text: Less starting material is wasted, which matters for cost and sustainability.
options.rationale: The specification gives both reasons: high atom economy matters for sustainable development and for economic reasons.

mcqs.stem: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2. Relative formula masses: CaCO3 = 100, CaO = 56, CO2 = 44. What is the atom economy for producing calcium oxide?

options.rationale: 56 / 100 x 100 = 56%: the relative formula mass of the desired product over the total for the reactants.
The atom economy for the carbon dioxide, chosen when the desired product is not fixed first.
Chosen by students who reason that since no atoms are lost, all the starting material must be used.
56 / 44 x 100, from comparing the two products with each other.

mcqs.stem: Fe2O3 + 3CO -> 2Fe + 3CO2. Mr(Fe2O3) = 160, Mr(CO) = 28, Ar(Fe) = 56. What is the atom economy for producing iron?

options.rationale: 56 / 244 x 100, from ignoring the 2 in front of Fe.
112 / 160 x 100, from using only the reactant that contains the iron.
112 / 188 x 100, from counting one CO instead of three in the reactant total.

mcqs.stem: What goes on the bottom line of a percentage atom economy calculation?

options.text: The relative formula mass of the reactant containing the desired product.
options.rationale: The other reactant is treated as a helper rather than as a starting material.

options.text: The relative formula masses of the reactants without the balancing numbers.
options.rationale: Coefficients are seen as bookkeeping for balancing rather than as multipliers of mass.

options.text: The relative formula masses of all the reactants shown in the equation.
options.rationale: The specification's equation uses the sum of the relative formula masses of all reactants from the equation.

options.text: The total mass of the reactants that was weighed out for the experiment.
options.rationale: Experimental masses are imported into a calculation taken from the equation alone.

mcqs.stem: Zn + H2SO4 -> ZnSO4 + H2. Ar(Zn) = 65, Mr(H2SO4) = 98, Mr(H2) = 2. What is the atom economy for producing hydrogen?

options.rationale: 2 / 65 x 100, from dividing by the zinc alone.
From counting products rather than masses: one of the two products is wanted.
The share taken by the zinc sulfate, or 100 minus the correct answer.

mcqs.stem: Two pathways make the same product. Pathway 1: atom economy 100%, yield 95%, fast. Pathway 2: atom economy 55%, yield 95%, fast, by-product sold as fertiliser. Which choice is better justified?

options.text: Pathway 1, because the same product is made from less starting material.
options.rationale: With yield and rate matched, the higher atom economy means less raw material is bought and less waste is made.

options.text: Pathway 2, because selling a by-product always outweighs a lower economy.
options.rationale: A single factor is promoted to a rule instead of being weighed against the others.

options.text: Pathway 2, because a lower atom economy gives it the higher percentage yield.
options.rationale: The two percentages are assumed to be linked, here inversely; the data give equal yields.

options.text: Pathway 1, because a 100% atom economy also guarantees that no product is lost.
options.rationale: Atom economy is read as a promise about the practical rather than about the equation.

mcqs.stem: Pathway A: atom economy 90%, reversible, reaches equilibrium at 12% yield, very slow. Pathway B: atom economy 60%, yield 90%, fast, by-product is useful. Why might B be chosen?

options.text: A has to be chosen, because atom economy is the measure that decides.
options.rationale: Atom economy is treated as decisive because it is presented as the greener measure.

options.text: B makes far more product per day and its by-product is still used.
options.rationale: Weighs rate, yield, equilibrium position and usefulness of by-products against A's higher atom economy, as the specification requires.

options.text: A is not possible at all, because a reversible reaction makes no product.
options.rationale: The reversible arrow is read as producing nothing, so A is dismissed for the wrong reason.

options.text: B is better because 60% atom economy means the product is 60% pure.
options.rationale: Atom economy is misread as a purity figure, which no data in the question supports.

mcqs.stem: N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3 in a reversible reaction. Mr values: N2 = 28, H2 = 2, NH3 = 17. The atom economy is 100% but the percentage yield is low. Why?

options.text: A 100% atom economy means the low percentage yield must be a measuring error.
options.rationale: The ceiling set by the equation is mistaken for what actually happened.

options.text: Atom economy and percentage yield are the same, so one figure has to be wrong.
options.rationale: The two measures are merged, so different values look like a contradiction.

options.text: Every reactant atom can reach the ammonia, but the reaction is incomplete.
options.rationale: 34 / 34 x 100 = 100% atom economy, while reversibility stops the reaction going to completion, so the yield is lower.

options.text: Ammonia escapes as a gas, so the true atom economy is well below 100%.
options.rationale: A practical loss is used to adjust a figure that comes only from the equation.

mcqs.stem: In which reaction is the atom economy for the named product 100%?

options.text: CaCO3 -> CaO + CO2, making calcium oxide
options.rationale: Picked when the carbon dioxide is not counted as taking a share of the starting material.

options.text: 2H2O2 -> 2H2O + O2, making oxygen
options.rationale: Chosen because no atoms are lost, so it seems that nothing has been wasted.

options.text: Zn + CuSO4 -> ZnSO4 + Cu, making copper
options.rationale: A displacement looks like a simple swap, so the sulfate that stays behind is overlooked.

options.text: C2H4 + H2O -> C2H5OH, making ethanol
options.rationale: There is only one product, so all the reactant mass, 28 + 18 = 46, appears in the ethanol, Mr 46.
